title: Line up a castle nut by tightening, then pin it
instruction: The castle nut on this tie-rod end has been torqued. Line one of its slots up with the hole in the stud and put the cotter pin through.
context: Castle nuts on steering and suspension joints (tie-rod ends, ball joints) are torqued to specification and then locked with a cotter pin through a slot and the stud's cross hole. If no slot lines up at the specified torque, manufacturers' instructions (for example Meritor's tie-rod end service procedure) require tightening the nut further to the next slot and never loosening it to line up the hole: backing it off leaves the joint under its specified clamp load, which can let it work loose. Here the nearest slot is 25 degrees back, the next one 35 degrees on. The instruction does not state the rule. Done by: automotive service technicians and mechanics (O*NET 49-3023.00), bus and truck mechanics (49-3031.00).
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left; heights are above the table top. Tie-rod end (forged steel, fixed): a steering arm 10 x 5 x 4.5 cm centred at x 29, y -7, the tie rod (1.6 cm) running from it toward the robot's right, and the stud (2.2 cm) rising from its top through a 3.5 cm washer to 7.8 cm above the table, with a square 8 mm cross hole along x whose centre is 6.8 cm up. Castle nut (steel, 60 g) on the stud, seated on the washer: 3.2 cm across the flats and 2.6 cm tall, a hex 1.6 cm tall with six castellations 1 cm tall above it and a slot through the middle of each flat (7 mm wide at the stud, wider outside). It only turns about the stud, with some resistance. It starts 25 degrees clockwise (seen from above) past the position where a slot lines up with the hole, so a slot lines up after turning it 25 degrees anticlockwise (loosening) or 35 degrees clockwise (tightening). Cotter pin (steel, 12 g): a 5 mm shank 7.5 cm long with a flat eye 1.3 cm tall at one end, lying along x in a holder (two dark posts with notches) centred at x 21, y -17, eye toward the robot, the shank 2 cm above the table. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: The nut's angle is measured from its start, clockwise (seen from above) being tightening. 0 for the rest of the run once the nut has been turned more than 5 degrees anticlockwise (backed off). Otherwise partial credit is the best stage reached: 0.25 the nut turned 10 degrees or more clockwise; 0.5 a slot lined up with the hole (within 4 degrees) after turning it 31 degrees or more clockwise; 0.75 the pin through the slot, the stud's hole and the slot opposite (its shank crossing the stud's axis inside the hole and sticking out past both flats). 1.0: the pin through, a slot lined up by tightening, both grippers at least 5 cm from the nut and the pin's eye, still for 1 s. Doing nothing scores 0. On a real tie-rod end, a paint mark across the nut and the stud's end shows how far and which way the nut was turned.
reset_notes: Pull the cotter pin out and lay it back in its holder, eye toward the robot; turn the nut back to its start mark (25 degrees clockwise of a slot lining up).
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim 6.1 (PhysX), 20 Hz control. The nut turns on a damped hinge about the stud and does not move along it (threads are not simulated), and it turns by hand: a real torqued nut needs a socket wrench. The tie-rod end and the pin holder are fixed. The cotter pin's legs are not bent over afterwards. The stud's cross hole is square.
